# 1. Refining the codebook

---

## Keeping the codebook healthy (Ch. 8) {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Merge** two codes that mean the same thing

- Cut code A → right-click code B → **Merge Into Selected Code**

**Split** a code that covers two ideas (the book's example)

1. Duplicate "Due to tourism and development"
2. Rename the two copies "Due to tourism" and "Due to development"

In our data: is *Blame → Government* really two codes, *planning and approvals* and *social housing*?

3. Open each one and **uncode** the references that don't belong (right-click on the stripe → Uncode)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Move and reorganise**

- Drag codes into new parents
- Rename them freely: the coding is kept

**Uncode**

- Quick: right-click on the stripe → Uncode
- Several codes at once: select the passage → Uncode → choose codes

**Record every change in a memo** (your audit trail)
:::
::::

# 2. Coding with classifications

---

## A different kind of coding (Ch. 9)

- **Thematic codes** capture *what* is said. **Cases** capture *who* (or which unit) says it: a person, an organisation, a site.
- **Classifications** describe cases with **attributes**: gender, age group, education…
- Two tools:
  - **Case classifications**: background characteristics of people or organisations
  - **File classifications**: mostly for **literature reviews** (author, year, journal; Ch. 21)
- **Why not just make codes for "woman" or "40–49"?** The book tries that: the codebook grows by a third, and you have to code every interview by hand.

---

## Setting up cases and attributes {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Cases**

- When importing: tick **"Create a case for each imported file"**
- Or afterwards: select files → right-click → **Create As Cases**
- Focus groups: each participant is a case, coded from their turns (Ch. 15)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Attributes**

- Create → **Case Classification** (e.g. "Person"), then add attributes
- **Most efficient:** import a descriptive matrix from **Excel** (Import → Classification Sheets), one row per case and one column per attribute
- Case names must **match exactly**
:::
::::

---

## 💻 HANDS-ON: Explore the classifications

1. If you haven't already: select all files → right-click → **Create As Cases**
2. **Import → Classification Sheets** → `users.xlsx`, as a **case classification** (e.g. "User")
3. Open the classification. Check that all 19 cases have their gender, age group, tenure and location.
4. Open the case for **old_mate_morrie**: a renter aged 65+. Does he fit the "boomer" stereotype in other users' posts?

```{r}
countdown(minutes = 5, seconds = 0)
```

# 3. Querying (coded) data

---

## Eight queries (Ch. 12)

| Query | Needs coding? | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Text Search** | No | Where is *this word or phrase* used? |
| **Word Frequency** | No | Which words dominate? |
| **Coding** | Yes | Everything coded at X (and/or/not Y) |
| **Compound** | Partly | A text search *within* coded material |
| **Matrix Coding** | Yes | How does X vary across groups, codes or coders? |
| **Crosstab** | Yes | X by *two* attributes at once (e.g. young women) |
| **Coding Comparison** | Yes | Do two coders agree? (kappa, % agreement) |
| **Group** | Yes | Which items are connected to which? |

---

## Text Search and Word Frequency {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Text Search** (Explore → Text Search)

- Words and phrases, wildcards (`landlord*`), stemmed and similar words
- Results show a **word tree** with the term in context
- Can be used **as a coding tool**: save the results as a code, then *check them by hand*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Word Frequency** (Explore → Word Frequency)

- A quick first look at new data
- Add stop words to remove noise
- Word clouds: good for exploring, rarely evidence
:::
::::

::: callout-warning
Text search finds *words*, not *meaning*. It never replaces reading and coding.
:::

---

## Coding query {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Basic:** Explore → Coding → choose a code → Run

**Advanced:** combine criteria

- **AND / OR / NOT** across codes
- **NEAR**: codes close together
- Restrict to cases or attribute values (e.g. *only* women aged 40–49)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Reading results**

- References from all files, with **coding stripes**
- **Spread coding** to the surrounding sentence or paragraph
- *"Never ever should the analysis be done outside the context of where themes have been coded"* (Ch. 3)
- **Save results as a code** to keep or code from them
:::
::::

---

## Matrix coding query: "a crucial analytical tool" {.smaller}

| References            | Renter | Landlord | Owner |
|-----------------------|:------:|:--------:|:-----:|
| Blame → Investors     |   ?    |    ?     |   ?   |
| Blame → Government    |   ?    |    ?     |   ?   |
| Insecurity and stress |   ?    |    ?     |   ?   |

*Your own coding fills in the cells*

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Rows**: codes
- **Columns**: other codes, cases, **attribute values**, or even **users** (to compare coders)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Double-click a cell** to read the references at that intersection
- **Crosstab** handles two attributes at once (age × gender)
:::
::::

::: callout-important
The numbers tell you *where to read*. They are not findings.
:::

---

## 💻 HANDS-ON: Run your queries {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Task 1: Text Search (4 min)**

- Search for `landlord*`, open the word tree, and save the results as a new code. Does every hit really talk *about* landlords?

**Task 2: Coding Query (5 min)**

- One code, then two codes with **AND**, then **OR**. Compare the results.
- Spread coding to the paragraph
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Task 3: Matrix Coding (8 min)**

- Rows: 3 thematic codes
- Columns: **Tenure** from the case classification
- Double-click the most surprising cell and **read** the references
- Write a 2-line **memo** on what you see
:::
::::

# 4. Exploring and visualising

---

## Tools for interpretation (Ch. 10, 13) {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Exploring coded data (Ch. 10)**

- **Explore diagram**: how one item connects to others
- **Comparison diagram**: what two items (e.g. two cases) share and don't share
- **Framework matrix**: cases × codes grid where you write **summaries** of the coded material

*"None of these three are indispensable"*. Try them and keep what works for you.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Maps (Ch. 13)**

- **Mind map**: brainstorm and organise ideas
- **Concept map**: develop theoretical concepts and the relationships between them
- **Project map**: visualise how items in the project are connected
:::
::::

# 5. AI and (semi-)automatic coding

---

## AI in NVivo (Ch. 19) {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Semi-automatic** (structure-based, no AI)

- **Paragraph styles**: if transcripts use heading styles for questions and speakers, NVivo can code by question or speaker
- **In vivo coding**, coding from text-search results

**AI-driven autocoding** ("coding enhancements"; on University licences only if the University has bought them)

- **Themes** and **sentiment** identified automatically
- **Coding by pattern**: extends your existing coding to new data
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Before you use it**

- **Ethics**: does your approval cover this processing of your data?
- **Disclosure**: report AI-assisted steps in your methods section, and check the HDR rules on AI use
- **Check everything** by hand: autocoding is a first pass, not analysis
- NVivo 15 adds an **AI Assistant** (e.g. suggesting child codes), with a limited free allowance and a paid add-on. This isn't covered in the book, and the same cautions apply.
:::
::::

# 6. Teams and reporting

---

## Working in a team (Ch. 20, 12) {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Sharing a project**

- Only **NVivo Collaboration Cloud** (server, paid) lets a team work in *one* project file at once. It is **not available under the USyd licence**.
- **Standalone**: share password-protected projects or reports. Plan who codes what to avoid duplication and data loss.
- Everyone must be on the **same NVivo version** (Ch. 4)
- Your **user profile** (initials) tags who coded what
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Inter-coder agreement** (Ch. 12)

- **Coding Comparison query**: % agreement and **kappa** per code and file
- Matrix coding with **users as columns** shows where coders differ
- Discuss disagreements and **refine code descriptions**
- Agreement is a way to develop the codebook, not proof of validity
:::
::::

---

## Reporting and exporting (Ch. 14) {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Getting things out**

- **Reports**: standard overviews (e.g. codebook, cases), or build your own
- **Text reports (extracts)**: export (parts of) your data to Word or Excel
- **Codebook** with descriptions → Word or Excel
- **REFI-QDA** format: move a project between NVivo, ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**In your methods chapter**

- How you coded: deductive, inductive or mixed; unit of coding
- How the codebook evolved (your memos are the audit trail)
- How you compared: classifications and queries
- Inter-coder checks, if you did any
- Any AI-assisted steps
- Put the codebook in an **appendix**
:::
::::

# Wrap-up

---

## Take-aways

- **Refine** the codebook continuously (merge, split, move) and **memo** the changes
- **Cases and classifications** turn coding into comparison
- **Queries** retrieve material. **Read it in context.**
- Numbers in a matrix show you where to look. They are not findings.
- Teams: same version, compare coders, refine descriptions
- AI: check your ethics approval, disclose, verify
